'''''Tillandsia recurvata''''', commonly known as '''small ballmoss'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TIRE|taxon=Tillandsia recurvata|accessdate=10 December 2015}}</ref> or '''ball moss''', is a [[flowering plant]] (not a true [[moss]]) in the family [[Bromeliaceae]] that grows upon larger host plants. It grows well in areas with low light, little airflow, and high humidity, which is commonly provided by southern shade trees, often the southern live oak (''[[Quercus virginiana]]'').<ref name = crow>{{cite video
| last = Crow
| first = William T
| date = 2000
| title = Ball Moss
| publisher = The Texas Agricultural Extension Service. L-5353
| access-date = 4 May 2008
| url = http://hays.agrilife.org/files/2011/08/ballmoss_1.pdf}}</ref> It is not a [[Parasitic plant|parasite]] like [[mistletoe]], but an [[epiphyte]] like its relative [[Spanish moss]].

''Tillandsia recurvata'' derives mainly physical support and not nutrition from its host; it [[photosynthesis|photosynthesizes]] its own food, absorbing water that collects on its leaves.<ref name = crow /> It obtains [[nitrogen]] from bacteria, and other minerals largely from blown dust.<ref>{{cite journal
|author1=Puente, Maria-Esther  |author2=Bashan, Yoav
 |name-list-style=amp |date=March 1994
| title = The desert epiphyte ''Tillandsia recurvata'' harbours the nitrogen-fixing bacterium ''Pseudomonas stutzeri''
| journal = Canadian Journal of Botany
| volume = 72
| number = 3

| pages = 406–8
| doi=10.1139/b94-054}}</ref> Though not a harmful parasite in the same sense as plants such as [[mistletoe]]s that feed on the sap of the host, ball moss may compete with a host tree for sunlight and some nutrients, and by restricting available surface area for new branch sprouts; however, except on stressed host trees (e.g., in some urban settings) it rarely has a noticeable effect on growth or health.<ref name = crow />

In [[Habit (biology)|habit]], ''Tillandsia recurvata'' tends to form a [[spheroid]] ranging in size from a [[golf ball]] to a [[soccer ball]], though this is actually a collection of multiple "pups" growing joined together. Several studies suggest that wind is the main agent of [[seed dispersal]].<ref name = crow /><ref>Victoriano-Romero, Elizabeth, et al. “Dispersal Limitation of Tillandsia Species Correlates with Rain and Host Structure in a Central Mexican Tropical Dry Forest.” ''PLOS One'', vol. 12, no. 2, Mar. 2017, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171614.</ref><ref>Bernal, Rocío, et al. “Habitat Preference of the Epiphyte Tillandsia Recurvata (Bromeliaceae) in a Semi-Desert Environment in Central Mexico.” ''Canadian Journal of Botany'', vol. 83, no. 10, 2005, pp. 1238–1247., doi:10.1139/b05-076.</ref><ref>Palací, Carlos A., et al. “The Seeds of Catopsis (Bromeliaceae: Tillandsioideae).” ''Systematic Botany'', vol. 29, no. 3, Jan. 2004, pp. 518–527., doi:10.1600/0363644041744473.</ref> It has not been demonstrated empirically that ''T. recurvata'' is capable of dispersal through animal-mediated vectors, such as [[Seed dispersal#Animals: epi- and endozoochory|epizoochory or endozoochory]]. Mature seeds have no apparent adhesive on the exterior, and very little nutrient supply to support sprouting, but, like many other epiphyte seeds, they are borne plentifully and are armed with fine, straight hairs that could well adhere to wet or clinging surfaces, such as rough bark, which would provide enough time for the seedlings to anchor themselves with their roots.<ref>Schimper, A.F.W.: Die epiphytische Vegetation Amerikas. Jena 1888</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.bio.utexas.edu/courses/bio406d/images/pics/brm/tillandsia_recurvata.htm | title=Tillandsia recurvata}}</ref> In fact, as shown in the accompanying photograph, they even grow plentifully on fences and telephone wires, together with occasional other species. 
[[File:Schimper-Tafel6.jpg|thumb|Comparison of a ''Tillandsia'' seed (number 9) with seeds of some other American epiphytic species]]
[[File:Tillandsia recurvata on electricity cables Tamaulipas.jpg|thumb|''Tillandsia recurvata'' growing on wires, together with another species, possibly ''Tillandsia usneoides'']]

Ball moss is sensitive to freezing, particularly when moist.<ref>{{cite thesis
| last = Hagar
| first = CF
| year = 1990
| title = The effect of water content, cooling rate, and growth temperature on the freezing temperature of 4 Tillandsia species
| degree = Masters
|url=https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/ETD-TAMU-1990-THESIS-H141
| publisher = [[Texas A&M University]]| hdl = 1969.1/ETD-TAMU-1990-THESIS-H141
}}</ref>

Ball moss is indigenous to the warmer regions of the [[Americas]]; it ranges from the [[southern United States]] to northern [[Argentina]] and [[Chile]].<ref>{{cite book
|author1=Correll, Donovan Stewart  |author2=Johnston, Marshall Conring
 |name-list-style=amp | year = 1970
| title = Manual of the Vascular Plants of Texas
| location = Renner, Texas
| publisher = Texas Research Foundation
| page = 356}}</ref>
The northernmost limit of its natural occurrence is coastal Georgia (where it is listed as a State "Special Concern" species), although it has been introduced into coastal South Carolina on landscaping trees.<ref>Weakley, Alan (2010). [http://www.herbarium.unc.edu/WeakleyFlora2010Mar.pdf ''Flora of the Southern and Mid-Atlantic States''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180722005826/http://www.herbarium.unc.edu/WeakleyFlora2010Mar.pdf |date=2018-07-22 }} University of North Carolina Herbarium. p161</ref> It has been reported in nature from [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Florida]], [[Louisiana]], [[Texas]], [[Arizona]], [[Mexico]], most of [[Central America|Central]] and [[South America]], and many of the islands in the [[West Indies]].<ref name=u>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=269621 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families, ''Tillandsia recurvata'']</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=222000401 Flora of North America, ''Tillandsia recurvata'' (Linnaeus) Linnaeus, Sp. Pl., ed. 2. 1: 410. 1762. ]</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Tillandsia%20recurvata.png Biota of North America Program, 2013 county distribution map]</ref> In the [[United States]], ball moss is considered unattractive by some, and many landowners attempt to remove these bromeliads from their trees using different chemical solutions.

==Uses==
''Tillandsia recurvata'' can be used as animal [[fodder]].{{Citation needed|date=May 2008}}

The [[Pima people|Pima]] of Mexico occasionally eat '''''T. recurvata''''' and ''[[Tillandsia erubescens|T. erubescens]]'' flowers due to their high sugar content.<ref name = bromeliads2011polibotanica/>
